covers.quote: Limit each paragraph to one topic
Start a new paragraph instead.
Introduction or summary paragraphs recap ideas covered in the content. Group sentences in these paragraphs by theme – for example, to help users understand how the content is structured.

rules.quote: Don’t introduce a new topic in the middle or at the end of a paragraph.
rules.violation_condition: a paragraph introducing more than one topic or theme instead of starting a new paragraph
when: Introduction or summary paragraphs recap ideas covered across the content and may group sentences by theme.
rules.why: G-1, G-4: The heading states the goal; the body sentence gives the actionable negative instruction.

covers.quote: Put paragraphs in the order that makes sense to the user

rules.quote: Order paragraphs in a logical sequence
rules.violation_condition: paragraphs arranged in an illogical or arbitrary order rather than a structured sequence (such as chronological steps, order of importance, cause/effect, problem/solution, or pros/cons)
rules.why: G-4: Heading and lead-in state the same principle; heading is absorbed.

covers.quote: Expand on the heading in the first paragraph
Use the first paragraph to make the purpose of your content easier to find in searches.

rules.quote: It should include a topic sentence and summarise the following paragraphs.
rules.violation_condition: the first paragraph under a heading fails to include a topic sentence or summarise the following paragraphs
when: Applies to the first paragraph under a heading.
rules.why: G-4: The body sentence specifies the requirement for the first paragraph under a heading.

covers.quote: Structure each paragraph well
To write an effective topic sentence, use active voice.

examples.note: Active voice topic sentence making the paragraph topic the grammatical subject.

parts.quote: Our rapid response team began operating in 2019 as a result of the 2018 stakeholder survey. The survey showed it took too long to repair damage.

examples.note: Subject of first sentence ('the survey') does not reflect the main topic of the paragraph ('the team').

parts.quote: A stakeholder survey in 2018 revealed dissatisfaction with the time taken to repair damage. Our rapid response team began operating in 2019.

examples.note: Paragraph starts with an explicit transition sentence linking to the previous paragraph.

parts.quote: … In summary, an effective policy strategy understands public needs, the purpose of the strategy and the desired strategic outcome.

To build on a robust policy strategy, it’s essential to evaluate and measure outcomes after implementation. Analyse performance metrics and gather user feedback regularly. And stay responsive: keep informed about societal trends and adapt where necessary …

rules.quote: The first sentence in each paragraph should be a topic or transition sentence.
rules.violation_condition: a paragraph whose first sentence neither states what the paragraph is about (topic sentence) nor connects the paragraph to the preceding one (transition sentence)
rules.why: G-1, G-2: The subsections on topic and transition sentences flesh out how to fulfil this single rule.

covers.quote: Be clear when using pronouns to start paragraphs
Take care if you start a paragraph with a pronoun. It should already be clear who or what the pronoun is referring to.

examples.note: Noun repeated in the new paragraph rather than starting with an ambiguous pronoun.

parts.quote: The initial amounts for appropriation in 2019–20 were up to:
$295 million for ordinary annual services
$380 million for other annual services.
The appropriations increased in March 2020 to account for unforeseen expenditures in relation to COVID-19.

examples.note: New paragraph starts with unclear demonstrative pronoun 'These'.

parts.quote: The initial amounts for appropriation in 2019–20 were up to:
$295 million for ordinary annual services
$380 million for other annual services.
These increased in March 2020 to account for unforeseen expenditures in relation to COVID-19.

rules.quote: If not, make sure to mention the noun in each paragraph before using the pronoun that substitutes the noun.
rules.specification: Do not start a paragraph with an ambiguous pronoun (especially demonstratives like 'these') unless the antecedent noun is clearly restated first.
rules.violation_condition: a pronoun starting a paragraph whose referent is unclear without having mentioned the noun first in that paragraph
when: When starting a paragraph with a pronoun whose referent is not already clear.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: The heading and preamble lead up to the rule requiring mention of the noun if the pronoun's antecedent is not clear.

covers.quote: Media releases and news articles have 1 or 2 sentences in a paragraph.
Content designed for mobile screens has no more than 2 or 3 sentences in a paragraph.
Reports (and other long-form content) usually have a limit of 6 sentences in a paragraph.
A paragraph can be one sentence, but be careful. Overusing single-sentence paragraphs reduces their effectiveness and can disrupt the flow of content.

rules.quote: Keep most paragraphs to 2 or 3 sentences
rules.specification: Keep paragraphs to 2 or 3 sentences generally; max 2 in media releases, max 3 in mobile content, max 6 in reports.
rules.violation_condition: paragraphs exceeding recommended sentence length limits: more than 2 sentences in news/media releases, more than 3 sentences in mobile/web content, or more than 6 sentences in reports/long-form content
when: Media releases and news articles have 1 or 2 sentences in a paragraph.

rules.why: G-1, G-2: The heading gives the general threshold, elaborated by content-specific limits in the bullet list.

rules.quote: Write clear sentences using a maximum of 25 words
rules.specification: Limit sentence length to 25 words or fewer.

rules.why: G-4: Clear numeric sentence-length rule stated in heading and body.
